distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for aplastic anemia. Acquired, immune, severe, very severe, hepatitis-associated, drug-induced, pregnancy-associated, inherited marrow-failure predisposition, PNH-associated, and clonal-evolution contexts are represented as risk, context, treatment-modifier, or future subtype axes rather than disease-name qualifiers.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell pool depletion
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: A reduced functional hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell compartment limits trilineage blood-cell production. The upstream trigger can vary without changing the first-layer aplastic anemia disease leaf.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Immune T-cell attack on hematopoietic progenitors
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Cytotoxic and cytokine-mediated immune activity suppresses or destroys hematopoietic progenitors in many presentations, explaining response to immunosuppression while not requiring a subtype label in the disease name.
The marrow space is depleted of hematopoietic cellularity and replaced by fat, producing a confirmatory workup pattern rather than a presentation-only requirement.
Reduced marrow output lowers neutrophils, platelets, red cells, and reticulocytes, often with inappropriately low reticulocyte response for the degree of anemia.
Low neutrophil reserve increases fever, invasive bacterial or fungal infection, and sepsis hazards, particularly when severe or prolonged.

Reduced platelet production produces bruising, petechiae, mucosal bleeding, and major bleeding hazards, with risk amplified by very low platelets and delivery, trauma, procedures, hypertension, or anticoagulant exposure.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Erythroid hypoproliferation and oxygen delivery failure
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Low red-cell production causes anemia, pallor, fatigue, exertional dyspnea, tachycardia, presyncope, and transfusion dependence.
Aplastic anemia can coexist with small PNH clones and can evolve toward myelodysplastic or leukemic clonal states. These are context and hazard axes, not required presentation evidence.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Immune-mediated progenitor injury can progressively deplete functional hematopoietic reserve.
Loss of hematopoietic progenitors yields hypocellular marrow with fatty replacement.
Insufficient stem-cell reserve directly limits production of red cells, neutrophils, and platelets.
Erythroid hypoproliferation lowers hemoglobin.
Reduced red-cell mass lowers hematocrit.
Hypocellular marrow gives an inappropriately low reticulocyte response.
The percent can be low or deceptively normal but is inadequate for anemia.
A low reticulocyte production index captures marrow hypoproliferation better than raw percent in severe anemia.
Marrow failure reduces leukocyte output.
Granulopoietic failure lowers absolute neutrophil count and strongly determines infection risk.
Megakaryocytic production failure lowers platelets.
Concurrent anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia define the presentation pattern.
Hypocellular marrow cellularity is a confirmatory marrow-failure finding.
Aplastic anemia lacks excess blasts; blast burden instead suggests a separate malignant marrow disease.
Anemia commonly causes fatigue, lethargy, and reduced effort tolerance.
Low hemoglobin produces pallor.
Reduced oxygen carrying capacity can cause exertional dyspnea.
Severe anemia can produce compensatory tachycardia.
Profound anemia can cause presyncope or syncope.
Neutropenia predisposes to febrile infection, though patients may present afebrile before infection occurs.
Fever can emerge from neutropenic infection but is not obligatory at initial presentation.
Severe neutropenia increases febrile neutropenia hazard.
Prolonged severe neutropenia increases invasive infection and sepsis hazard.
Low platelets produce easy bruising and ecchymoses.
Low platelets produce petechiae and purpura.
Severe thrombocytopenia can cause gingival, oral, nasal, urinary, or gastrointestinal bleeding.
Very low platelet counts increase major bleeding hazard.
Severe thrombocytopenia can rarely cause fatal intracranial hemorrhage, especially with additional bleeding-risk contexts.
Small PNH clones can coexist with aplastic anemia and may modify thrombosis and treatment context.
Abnormal cytogenetic clones may indicate clonal evolution or a competing marrow disease and require longitudinal interpretation.
Long-term marrow failure can evolve toward myelodysplastic syndrome or leukemia.
Severe infection and sepsis are major mortality drivers in aplastic anemia.
Major bleeding and intracranial hemorrhage can be fatal.
Deeper and more persistent marrow failure worsens survival when definitive hematopoietic recovery is not achieved.
Clonal evolution and clinically significant PNH can worsen long-term outcome.

axes.clinical_meaning: Low hemoglobin reflects erythroid hypoproliferation and drives fatigue, pallor, dyspnea, and transfusion need.
Low hematocrit parallels anemia severity.
Low absolute reticulocyte count indicates hypoproliferative marrow output.
Reticulocyte percent can be low or deceptively normal but is inadequate when anemia is severe.
Low index captures inadequate marrow response after correction for anemia.
Leukopenia often accompanies marrow failure.
Neutropenia is central to infection and sepsis hazard.
Relative neutropenia may be seen with marrow failure and helps interpret absolute neutrophil count.
Relative lymphocytosis can appear when neutrophils are disproportionately reduced.
Thrombocytopenia drives bruising and bleeding hazards.
Joint low red-cell, neutrophil, and platelet production pattern. Runtime should avoid counting this together with all component CBC axes unless explicitly modeled as a derived pattern.
Fatigue, weakness, lethargy, or reduced effort tolerance from anemia and systemic illness.
Clinical pallor from severe anemia.
Exertional dyspnea can result from severe anemia.
Profound anemia can cause lightheadedness or presyncope.
Bruising reflects thrombocytopenic bleeding tendency.
Petechiae or purpura can occur from thrombocytopenia.
Gingival, oral, nasal, urinary, gastrointestinal, or uterine bleeding can occur when platelets are very low.
Fever may arise from neutropenic infection or from a triggering viral context, but afebrile presentation is also common.
Temperature can remain normal unless infection or another inflammatory context is present.
Tachycardia can reflect severe anemia, fever, or sepsis.
Blood pressure is often preserved unless bleeding, sepsis, or comorbid cardiovascular context emerges.
Aplastic anemia usually lacks pathologic lymphadenopathy; presence should raise competing disease or context.
Aplastic anemia usually lacks splenomegaly; marked splenomegaly suggests another process.
Aplastic anemia usually lacks hepatomegaly unless a separate liver, viral, or infiltrative context exists.
LDH is often normal or mildly abnormal; high LDH suggests hemolysis, PNH, tissue injury, or another disease.
Creatinine is not a core aplastic anemia axis but affects treatment tolerability and differential diagnosis.
ALT can be normal in many cases or elevated in hepatitis-associated or drug-related contexts.
AST can be normal or elevated depending on liver or systemic context.
Bilirubin is often normal unless hemolysis, PNH, liver disease, or transfusion-related complications are present.
Ferritin can reflect transfusion-related iron burden or inflammatory context; it is not a core presentation discriminator for aplastic anemia.

axes.display_name: Bone marrow cellularity percent in aplastic anemia
axes.clinical_meaning: Hypocellular marrow is confirmatory and should usually stay out of presentation-only ranking.
Aplastic anemia should not have excess blasts; elevated blasts indicate another or additional marrow disease.
Small PNH clones can coexist with aplastic anemia; large or hemolytic clones add treatment and hazard context.
Abnormal cytogenetics require clonal-evolution or competing-disease interpretation and should not be mandatory for presentation ranking.
Viral contexts such as hepatitis, EBV, CMV, HIV, or parvovirus can trigger or mimic marrow failure and affect treatment timing.
Medication or toxin context can modify management and causality without narrowing the disease name.
Pregnancy changes transfusion, infection, bleeding, delivery, and transplant timing context but is not part of the disease name.
Donor availability, age, comorbidity, pregnancy, infection, and center resources determine whether hematopoietic stem-cell transplantation is feasible.
Active infection, renal function, liver function, frailty, pregnancy, and prior therapy modify immunosuppressive therapy feasibility.

axes.display_name: Febrile neutropenia hazard in aplastic anemia
axes.clinical_meaning: Event hazard for fever during severe neutropenia.
Event hazard for invasive infection or sepsis driven by neutropenia and immunosuppression context.
Major bleeding hazard from severe thrombocytopenia and bleeding-risk contexts.
Catastrophic bleeding hazard downstream of severe thrombocytopenia and major bleeding context.

axes.display_name: Clonal evolution hazard in aplastic anemia
axes.clinical_meaning: Long-term event hazard for MDS, AML, or clinically important clonal evolution.
Lifespan outcome hazard emerging from marrow-failure depth, infection, bleeding, treatment feasibility, age, and clonal evolution.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both are jointly driven by erythroid marrow output, but neither should be treated as directly causing the other in ranking.
Severe anemia can cause compensatory tachycardia.
Lower ANC sharply increases febrile neutropenia hazard.
Lower ANC increases invasive infection and sepsis hazard.
Febrile neutropenia can transition to sepsis depending on pathogen, prophylaxis, and treatment speed.
Sepsis is a major near-term mortality pathway.
Lower platelet count increases major bleeding hazard.
Severe bleeding pressure can include intracranial hemorrhage as a catastrophic event.
Intracranial hemorrhage strongly increases mortality hazard.
Lower marrow cellularity supports more severe pancytopenia when used in post-workup mode.
Clonal evolution worsens long-term survival and treatment path.

treatments.clinical_role: Definitive hematopoietic rescue when donor, age, comorbidity, pregnancy, infection, and center context permit.

treatments.display_name: Horse ATG plus cyclosporine plus eltrombopag
treatments.clinical_role: Immune and hematopoietic rescue strategy when transplant is not immediately feasible or is not selected.
Alternative immunosuppressive regimen depending on local availability, prior therapy, and patient context.
Calcineurin inhibitor immune suppression, usually contextualized with combination therapy or special circumstances.
Thrombopoietin-receptor agonist support of residual hematopoiesis, often used in combination or refractory contexts.
Temporary oxygen-delivery support; does not reshape the marrow-failure landscape.
Temporary bleeding-risk reduction during severe thrombocytopenia, bleeding, or procedure or delivery contexts.

treatments.display_name: Broad-spectrum antimicrobial therapy for febrile neutropenia
treatments.clinical_role: Treatment of suspected or documented neutropenic infection according to local microbiology and patient context.
Contextual neutrophil support during severe neutropenia or infection; benefit depends on residual marrow reserve and treatment plan.
Risk reduction while neutropenia persists; specific agents depend on local pathogens and patient toxicities.

present.clinical_rationale: Older age reduces physiologic reserve and often narrows transplant or immunosuppression tolerability.
Pregnancy is a management context, not a disease-name restriction; delivery can amplify thrombocytopenic bleeding hazard.
Viral illnesses can precede or mimic marrow failure and can raise fever or transaminases depending on the virus.

risk_factors.display_name: Culprit drug or toxin exposure context

present.clinical_rationale: Medication or toxin exposure can be an upstream context without narrowing the disease name.
ANC near zero sharply increases febrile neutropenia and invasive infection hazards.
Very low platelet counts increase major bleeding and rare intracranial hemorrhage hazards.
PNH clone size is a measured context axis and can coexist with aplastic anemia.
Abnormal cytogenetics can signal clonal evolution or a competing marrow disease and should be interpreted longitudinally.
Documented infection during neutropenia raises sepsis hazard and changes treatment timing.

supportive_care.clinical_role: Avoid trauma, unnecessary antiplatelet or anticoagulant exposure, and invasive procedures when possible.
Reduce infection exposure and speed fever evaluation while ANC is low.

supportive_care.display_name: Irradiated and leukoreduced blood products when indicated
supportive_care.clinical_role: Support transfusion needs while reducing alloimmunization and transfusion-associated complications according to transplant plan and local policy.

supportive_care.display_name: Monitoring for clonal evolution and PNH
supportive_care.clinical_role: Longitudinal marrow, cytogenetic, and PNH evaluation when clinically appropriate.
Monitor chronic transfusion burden and hepatic context.
